clue.text: Lear's affliction created mostly by head

indicators.note: 'mostly' asks for most of a word rather than all of it, so the final letter is left behind.

parts.note: 'created' is MADE, and most of MADE is its first three letters
a ness is a headland, the ending of British place names like Sheerness, and 'by' sets it alongside

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's king is diagnosed as though his trouble were self-made, something cooked up in his own head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' looks like an instruction to take a first letter. It is a noun instead, the geographical ness that ends so many coastal place names.
explanation.definitionFit: King Lear loses his reason on the heath, so the state the play is remembered for is the affliction named here.

clue.text: I hear setter's hot beverage is strong

indicators.note: 'I hear' says the solver is being told something by ear, so what follows is spelled from its sound.

parts.note: the setter refers to himself, so 'setter's' is 'my', and the hot beverage is tea

explanation.surface: Someone reports that the person who writes the puzzle takes their hot drink strong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' is the crossword's word for whoever wrote the clue, so 'setter's' is a first-person possessive; the drink beside it is the ordinary British cuppa.
explanation.definitionFit: A mighty blow or a mighty river is simply a strong one; the two adjectives are plain synonyms.

clue.text: Party of America supplying dimwit

parts.note: a do is a party — a works do, a birthday do
the clue's own two letters, taken at face value
US is the standard short form of the United States

explanation.surface: An American political party is credited with turning out an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: The little word 'of' is not joinery here but two letters kept whole, which is why the charade reads as an ordinary phrase instead of a list of parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A doofus is American slang for a fool, so it meets 'dimwit' as an informal name for someone slow on the uptake.

clue.text: Driving out evil energy, replacing nothing troubling

indicators.note: 'replacing' means one letter stands in for another rather than simply being added to what is there.

parts.note: driving an evil spirit out of someone is exorcising them
E is the physicist's symbol for energy, and it is the letter moving in
the round letter that stands for nothing is the one giving up its place

explanation.surface: An exorcism in which energy is swapped in for nothing at all, and the ritual goes badly.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the very last word, and it is the formal sense of 'exercise' meaning to worry someone — the question exercising the committee.
explanation.definitionFit: What is exercising you is what is troubling you — the sense of 'exercise' meaning to occupy and worry the mind.

clue.text: Change key

definitions.meaning: a change of position, opinion or working hours — the noun, and also the verb
read literally: one of the keys on a keyboard, the one held down for capitals

explanation.surface: A musician is being told to modulate partway through the piece.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses sit side by side with no joinery at all, which is why the clue is only two words long — the shortest clues in a puzzle are nearly always double definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A shift is a change of position or opinion, and Shift is also the keyboard key held down for capitals — two unrelated senses.

clue.text: Flourish from magician, making ring disappear

indicators.note: a disappearance is the vanishing act, so the letter named just before it is gone from the word

parts.note: Prospero is the magician who raises the storm in The Tempest
a ring is the letter O, and this is the letter conjured away

explanation.surface: A conjuror's showy gesture on stage, with a ring vanishing between his fingers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flourish' wants to be the magician's sweep of the hand. It is the verb meaning to thrive, and it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To prosper is to flourish: both verbs mean to thrive, though 'flourish' also carries the showy stage sense the surface wants.

clue.text: Remarkable things: a mixture of hope 'n' amen!

indicators.note: a mixture has had its ingredients stirred together, so the letters that follow arrive in no fixed order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A recipe of sorts: stir a little hope together with an amen and see what wonders come out.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophes round 'n' make it look like decoration from a phrase such as rock 'n' roll, and it is a plain letter of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Phenomena are occurrences striking enough to be worth remarking on, so the plural noun answers a plural definition exactly.

clue.text: Pledge made by prisoner of hero at Hyperborea

indicators.note: a prisoner is held inside its captor, so the letters wanted are locked up within the words named next.

parts.note: four consecutive letters run across the gap between two of these words

explanation.surface: A promise extracted from a captive held by a hero in a far northern land.
explanation.walkthrough: Hyperborea is the Greeks' mythical country beyond the north wind, which is what lets the clue read as a scrap of legend rather than as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: An oath is a formal sworn promise — the oath of allegiance sense, not the swear-word one — which is what a pledge is.

clue.text: Friend cradling decapitated Trojan close to chest

indicators.note: a decapitated name has had its head cut off, so the letter it starts with never arrives.
to cradle something is to hold it in your arms, so one word closes right round another.

parts.note: a pal is a friend, and these three letters split to make the outside
the Trojan is Hector, the prince who leads Troy's defence in the Iliad, minus his first letter

explanation.surface: A friend holds a beheaded Trojan warrior tight against his own ribs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to chest' reads as the end of the surface picture, and it is the definition — an anatomical adjective rather than the description of a hug.
explanation.definitionFit: Pectoral means belonging to the chest — the pectoral muscles, or a bishop's pectoral cross, both sitting right on it.

clue.text: Freed soldier survived swallowing drug

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army corps whose men are the sappers

indicators.note: whatever is swallowed ends up inside the swallower, so the letter goes within the word before it.

parts.note: to have survived is to have lived, and this word opens up to take a letter
E is ecstasy, the crossword's default drug

explanation.surface: A soldier who came through and is still on something is let go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freed' points at the duty sense of the verb rather than the emotional one, which is the sense the surface's survivor pushes you towards.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier relieved of duty has been freed from it; the answer is the past participle in that sense, not the comforted one.

clue.text: The earth? Throw into empty grave

indicators.note: 'into' puts one thing within another, so the throw lands inside the word that follows.
an emptied word keeps only its outer walls, everything between them having been cleared out.

parts.note: GRAVE hollowed out keeps only the letters at its two ends
a lob is a throw, the high gentle kind

explanation.surface: A mourner lobbing something into a grave that has already been cleared out.
explanation.walkthrough: A burial and a planet share one short sentence, and 'The earth?' sits at the front where a solver expects the story to begin rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The globe is a standing name for the earth as a whole, as in 'travel the globe'; the question mark flags it as one name among several.

clue.text: Dromio or Antipholus potentially land in it twice by accident

indicators.note: something done by accident comes out wrong, and letters that come out wrong are no longer in the order given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, thirteen letters

explanation.surface: Two characters from a farce who keep landing in the same trouble twice over, by pure mishap.
explanation.walkthrough: Dromio and Antipholus are the two pairs of brothers in The Comedy of Errors. 'Twice' looks like an instruction to double something and is thirteen letters of plain fodder instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The Comedy of Errors gives both Dromio and Antipholus a brother indistinguishable from him, so either name is one example of the thing defined.

clue.text: Curtailment of holiday (3rd-8th) after travelling chest's end falls off

indicators.note: an end falling off is the last letter dropping away from the word it belonged to.
'after' means the letters just described come behind the ones still to be found, so the holiday piece lands second.

parts.note: a travelling chest is a trunk, and it loses the letter at its end
a holiday is a vacation, and the third to the eighth of its letters are the ones wanted

explanation.surface: Someone's holiday is cut short when the end falls off their travelling chest.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed '(3rd-8th)' reads as holiday dates in the surface. It is an instruction: count into the word for a holiday and take that run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nouns name the act of cutting something short before it reaches its proper end, so one stands in for the other.

clue.text: Left because of almost nothing

indicators.note: 'almost' stops just short of the whole word, so its final letter never arrives.

parts.note: L is the standard short form of left, as marked on a pair of gloves
'because of' is 'over', as in a quarrel over money, stopped one letter short

explanation.surface: Somebody walked out on account of the merest trifle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the definition of a departure and is one letter of wordplay; the definition is the last word, and it is a tennis score.
explanation.definitionFit: Love is the tennis scorer's word for no points at all, said to come from l'oeuf, the French egg shaped like a zero.

clue.text: Maybe branches hang on over generations

indicators.note: in a down entry the piece written over another sits directly above it, so it starts the answer.

parts.note: to append is to hang something on the end of what is already there
ages are the long stretches of time the surface calls generations

explanation.surface: Family branches that have somehow hung on down the generations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' is the setter flagging a definition by example: branches are one sort of thing that hangs off something bigger, not the only sort.
explanation.definitionFit: An appendage is anything that hangs off a larger body, and branches are one kind — 'maybe' flags the definition as by example.

clue.text: Starter of soup, fish second, fruit compote finally for Anne's husband perhaps

indicators.note: the starter is the first course of a meal, so what is taken is the first letter of the word.

parts.note: the opening letter of soup, the course a meal starts with
hake is a food fish of the cod family, common on British menus
s is the standard abbreviation for a second of time
the fruit is a pear, and it goes in whole

indicators.note: 'finally' points at the very last letter of the word standing before it.

parts.note: the last letter of compote

explanation.surface: A menu recited in order: soup to start, then fish, then a fruit compote to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: Five pieces hide as a set meal, and the join between courses is where the letters change hands. 'Perhaps' is honest: plenty of Annes have husbands.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Hathaway married the playwright from Stratford, so 'perhaps' admits he is one example of a man who is Anne's husband.

clue.text: Writer reporting parliamentary assents gets permit

parts.note: a writer is an author

indicators.note: reporting is repeating aloud what was said, so the second piece is spelled the way it sounds.

parts.note: in the Commons a vote in favour is an aye, and the ayes said out loud are the ending of a verb

explanation.surface: A journalist writing up the ayes of a Commons division is handed a pass for it.
explanation.walkthrough: The -ise ending of an English verb sounds exactly like the ayes counted in a parliamentary division, which is the whole of the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: To authorise something is to permit it officially, the on-paper version of giving permission rather than the casual one.

clue.text: Ugly stripe concealing alien's knick-knacks!

indicators.note: something ugly is misshapen, and letters made misshapen no longer sit in their proper order.
to conceal something is to hide it inside, so one piece ends up buried within the other.

parts.note: these six letters resettled, then split to make the outside
ET is the crossword's standard alien, after the film

explanation.surface: The stripes on something ugly turn out to have an extraterrestrial hiding among them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ugly' opens the clue as a description and works as the shuffle instruction, and what it shuffles ends up meaning very nearly the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: A 'pretty' used as a noun is a small ornamental thing, so the plural names the trinkets on a shelf — a slightly old-fashioned use.

clue.text: Boring piece I hone endlessly following morning drive

indicators.note: endlessly means without ends, so the word gives up the letter at each of them.
a follower walks behind, so the pieces named before it are written after the morning.

parts.note: AM marks the hours before noon
the bit is the piece of a drill that does the boring
the clue's own letter, taken straight
HONE surrenders the letter at each end

explanation.surface: A dull object somebody keeps sharpening for ever, after a morning at the wheel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' is not the surface's tedium but a hole being drilled, and 'drive' at the end is not the motoring one — both words change meaning between the story and the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: Drive here is the personal push that makes someone want to get on, which is what ambition is — not the motoring sense the surface offers.

clue.text: Argue against Sartre and Monet in review

indicators.note: a review goes back over its material and reorders it, so the names come out rearranged.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: A philosopher and a painter reconsidered side by side in a piece of French criticism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Review' is exactly the kind of word that could mean turn round; here it means go over again and reorder. The two Frenchmen have nothing to do with the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: To remonstrate is to argue against something to the person responsible, protesting rather than merely disagreeing.

clue.text: Tranquil moon goddess changes sides

indicators.note: a change here is a swap and not an addition: one letter steps out so another can step in.

parts.note: Selene is the Greek goddess who drives the moon across the sky
the sides are left and right, L and R, and the name's L is traded for the other

explanation.surface: A moon goddess so unruffled that she switches allegiance without anyone minding.
explanation.walkthrough: Left and right are L and R in almost every cryptic, which is what makes 'changes sides' an instruction about one letter rather than about loyalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Serene means calm and untroubled, the settled sense of tranquil rather than the merely quiet one.

clue.text: Words spoken privately since ill-omened day

parts.note: 'as' stands in for 'since' in the causal sense — as it was raining, we stayed in
the Ides of March is the date the soothsayer warns Caesar about

explanation.surface: A remark muttered under the breath ever since one unlucky date on the calendar.
explanation.walkthrough: The ides were only the middle of any Roman month; it is Caesar's assassination on the ides of March that makes one of them ill-omened.
explanation.definitionFit: In the theatre an aside is a line delivered to the audience and not to the other characters on stage, so asides are words spoken privately.

clue.text: See 10
Delivery of blade and nastily snide son lead to immoral actions

definitions.note: The definition is plural while the answer is a singular abstract noun; the setter is using the plural for sordid conduct taken as a whole.

indicators.note: done nastily, letters come out badly ordered rather than in the order they were handed over.
a speaker's delivery is how words leave the mouth, so this piece is spelled from its sound.

parts.note: the blade is a sword, and English has never sounded the w in that word
the five letters of the clue's own word, resettled
s is the usual abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A blade handed over, plus a spiteful man's boy, between them producing something thoroughly seedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Sword is one of the few English words with a silent w, and that silence is what lets 'Delivery' turn a blade into four letters worth building on.
explanation.definitionFit: Sordidness is squalid, self-seeking behaviour — the moral grubbiness that immoral actions add up to.

clue.text: Fancy doctor exfoliates and moisturises initially

parts.note: Dr is the everyday written title for a doctor

indicators.note: 'initially' keeps only the letter each of the named words begins with.

parts.note: the opening letters of the three words, kept in the order given

explanation.surface: A skincare routine — exfoliate, then moisturise — prescribed by an elegant doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' reads as an adjective describing the doctor, which is what the beauty-counter surface wants; it is the definition, and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A fancy is something the mind makes up, and a dream is exactly that in its daydreaming sense rather than its sleeping one.

clue.text: 14's pointless facial hair

indicators.note: a point is a compass point, and pointless means the word gives up the letter that names one.

parts.note: the facial hair is a beard

explanation.surface: The playwright's whiskers dismissed as serving no purpose whatever.
explanation.walkthrough: Compass points are the crossword's favourite letters to steal, so 'pointless' nearly always means one of N, S, E or W has been taken out.
explanation.definitionFit: The playwright at 14 across is known as the Bard of Avon, so the answer is the standing nickname for him.

clue.text: Fake current Lloyd Webber musical with brief interval making a comeback

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the word arrives without its final letter.

parts.note: I is the physicist's symbol for electric current

indicators.note: a comeback is a return the way you came, so those letters are read from the far end back.

parts.note: Evita is Lloyd Webber's musical about Eva Peron
an interval is a stretch of time, docked of its last letter

explanation.surface: An electrified revival of a Lloyd Webber show, its interval cut short, is written off as counterfeit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making a comeback' does two jobs at once: it is what a revived musical does, and it is the instruction to read the back half of the wordplay the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: Something imitative is copied from a model rather than original, which is the sense in which a fake is fake.

clue.text: Consented to take top off, resulting in desire

indicators.note: the top of a word is the letter it opens with, a shade loose in an across entry, and that letter comes away.

parts.note: to have consented is to have agreed

explanation.surface: Someone agreed to take their top off, and what it produced was appetite rather than admiration.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's top is a garment, which is the whole of the misdirection: a word wears one too, and it is the letter the word begins with.
explanation.definitionFit: Greed is desire taken past its fair share — the same appetite as the plain word, turned excessive.

clue.text: Trespass originally every day, in other words indefinitely

parts.note: to trespass, in the biblical sense of the Lord's Prayer, is to sin

indicators.note: a word's origin is where it starts, so each of the two words named gives up only its opening letter.

parts.note: the opening letters of the two words that follow the instruction
i.e. is what you write for 'that is', the phrase that puts something in other words

explanation.surface: Somebody owns up to trespassing every single day, and then rephrases the confession.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a Latin tag from court reports, where a case adjourned with no date fixed may never be heard again. The comma is punctuation for the surface, not a break in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Sine die is lawyers' Latin for 'without a day': a hearing adjourned sine die is put off with no date set, that is, indefinitely.

clue.text: Gains power over turbulent streams

indicators.note: turbulent water churns and tumbles, and letters churned like that come to rest in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: Somebody getting the better of a stretch of fast, rough water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Power over turbulent streams' reads as one idea, the taming of a river, so the seven letters sitting in plain sight at the end are easy to walk straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: To master something is to gain power over it — mastering a skill, a horse or a temper — taken as the verb, not the noun.
